note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — KLEINGRASS BUNCH
tiles.details: Kleingrass is an introduced African forage perennial, sometimes shortly rhizomatous, with an open 4–30 cm branching panicle. USDA and CC0 panels 0–1 teach the broad habit but do not expose roots. Harry Rose's panel 6 actually exposes a rooted knotty crown with attached fibrous roots from AUSTRALIAN var. makarikariense; this is real structural evidence, NOT a locally vouchered Texas root-to-head specimen. Never diagnose from pasture setting or one distant silhouette.
tiles.short: Introduced perennial: trace the fine open panicle to a firm, knotty rooted tuft.
tiles.status: VISIBLE HABIT — ROOTED LOCAL CROWN NOT VERIFIED

tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR
tiles.details: Open the blade–sheath junction and distinguish the actual membranous ligule rim from adjacent hairs. Flora of China describes about 0.5–1 mm while VicFlora gives about 0.5–2.5 mm across treatments. Physically archived Harry Rose AUSTRALIAN var. makarikariense panel 2 shows a real inner ligule region and visible fringe hairs; panel 4 shows the actual exterior collar junction. Existing arrows mark visible hairs or gross junction, NOT a measured membrane tip or a Texas variety.
tiles.short: Ciliate-edged membranous ligule, roughly 0.5–2.5 mm across treatments.
tiles.status: EXISTING VARIETY MACROS — TEXAS MEASURED LIGULE HOLD

tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE MATURE SPIKELETS
tiles.details: Follow an intact flowering branch to a mature spikelet and measure 5–10 specimens with a 1-mm scale. The real Harry Rose var. makarikariense spikelet photograph provides source-labelled reproductive context but does not independently establish dimensions or local Texas identity. A thin pedicel is NOT an awn.
tiles.short: Solitary pedicelled, awnless spikelets commonly ~2–3.2 mm.
tiles.status: SOURCE MEASUREMENTS — LOCAL SCALE PHOTO MISSING

tiles.heading: 04 · OPEN GLUMES AND LEMMAS
tiles.details: Under 10–20×, separate the short cufflike lower glume (usually 1-veined, sometimes to 3) from the upper approximately full-length 7–9-veined glume. The lower floret is staminate in cited treatments, with membranous lemma and palea; the upper fertile lemma is firm, shiny and approximately 1.5–2.5 mm, enclosing its palea. These are published characters, NOT proven by existing gallery pixels. Do not draw microscopic arrows until the parts are actually resolved.
tiles.short: Lower glume ~0.7–1 mm; upper glume near spikelet length; no true awns.

tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Compare rooted growth, true collar, mature spikelets and flowering architecture together. Native Panicum hallii is usually a smaller stiff basal tuft; native P. virgatum typically has scaly rhizomes and a dense triangular white hair patch at the blade base; P. capillare is a conspicuously hairy annual with an extremely diffuse head. Size, leaf color and habitat alone do not certify any of these species.
tiles.short: Hall's panicgrass is usually smaller/glaucous; switchgrass has a white blade-base hair triangle.
tiles.status: COMPARISON KEY — MATCHED LOCAL SPECIMENS NEEDED

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY PHOTO AND QA GATE
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: one source-vouchered Texas flowering plant with connected rooted crown and full panicle (cm scale); opened true inner ligule with 1-mm ruler; attached mature 2–3.2 mm spikelets with separately measured lower and upper glumes, lower staminate lemma/palea and hardened upper fertile lemma/palea (10–20×); same-scale local P. hallii and P. virgatum comparisons. NEEDS_SITE_QA: verify SIX physically archived species JPEGs and EIGHT panels (seven target or Australian-variety, one P. hallii OTHER-species), USDA/CC0/CC BY 2.0 rights, Harry Rose Australian variety labels, all existing visible-only arrows and mobile gallery. Do not mark FINISHED or infer Hays provenance.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS; existing licensed variety images are NOT Texas vouchers.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: KLEINGRASS: INTRODUCED African perennial forage TUFT, often tall and knotty at its center, with fine open branching panicles. Look for firm basal perennial growth, then confirm Panicum spikelet anatomy and collar. Existing two real photos show general habit, NOT precise ligule, glume length or crown cross section; never treat the naturalized Texas presence as county-native evidence.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: ARCHIVED EVIDENCE: panels 0–1 teach the overall forage habit; panel 6 is an ACTUAL lifted root crown with fibrous roots photographed by Harry Rose in Australia as var. makarikariense. This corrects the old 'no photographed roots' claim but does not provide a Texas rooted voucher. Panels 2 and 4 show true ligule-region hairs and exterior collar respectively, without a measured membrane tip.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Open the blade–sheath junction and distinguish the actual membranous ligule rim from adjacent hairs. Flora of China describes about 0.5–1 mm while VicFlora gives about 0.5–2.5 mm across treatments. Physically archived Harry Rose AUSTRALIAN var. makarikariense panel 2 shows a real inner ligule region and visible fringe hairs; panel 4 shows the actual exterior collar junction. Existing arrows mark visible hairs or gross junction, NOT a measured membrane tip or a Texas variety.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Follow an intact flowering branch to a mature spikelet and measure 5–10 specimens with a 1-mm scale. The real Harry Rose var. makarikariense spikelet photograph provides source-labelled reproductive context but does not independently establish dimensions or local Texas identity. A thin pedicel is NOT an awn.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Panicum virgatum: Switchgrass is native, rhizomatous, and has a characteristic hairy collar; Kleingrass is introduced and typically has a firm knotty base. Panicum hallii: Hall's panicum is smaller, glaucous and native, with a more compact stiff-branched panicle.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.caption: The photographer actually lifted the basal crown with roots attached. Follow the old papery basal leaf sheaths downward to the firm knotty perennial center, then out into fibrous roots. This makes the perennial growth form teachable; no rhizome internodes can be precisely measured here. Australian var. makarikariense only, not a Hays County voucher.
